rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recognizing the night’s sanctity shields a believer from unworthy thoughts and inclinations.
rows.anchor: realization of the sanctity of this night acts as a shield against unworthy thoughts and inclinations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad allows “Almightiness” or “Majesty” as alternatives for the night’s name, identifying it as the night of Muhammad’s first revelation; traditions place it among Ramadan’s last ten nights, probably the twenty-seventh, thirteen years before the Hijrah.
rows.anchor: describing the night on which the Prophet received his first revelation

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: The thousand months are those in which no comparable night occurred.
rows.anchor: in which there was no similar night" (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form tanazzalu conveys repetition, frequency, or multitude, supporting Ibn Kathir’s rendering that the angels descend in hosts.
rows.anchor: The grammatical form tanazzalu implies repetition, frequency or multitude; hence - as suggested by Ibn Kathir -

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruh here means divine inspiration; Asad identifies this as the Qur’an’s earliest use of the term in that sense.
rows.anchor: The present instance is undoubtedly the earliest example of the Qur'anic use of this term in the sense of

rows.speaker: Mujahid
rows.claim: Mujahid, quoted by Ibn Kathir, understands salam as salvation that secures the believer from spiritual evil.
rows.anchor: it makes the believer secure from all spiritual evil: thus Mujahid (as quoted by Ibn Kathir)

rows.speaker: some authorities
rows.claim: Some authorities classify the surah as Medinan, while many others regard it as a late Meccan revelation; its title word occurs at the end of verse 1.
rows.anchor: many others regard it as a late Meccan revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the verse to mean that deniers among scriptural communities and polytheists are not condemned before the full evidence of truth reaches them.
rows.anchor: should ever be abandoned [by Him] ere there comes unto them the [full] evidence of the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists named here include idol-worshippers and animists who have no revealed scripture to rely upon.
rows.anchor: idol-worshippers or animists (in the anthropological sense of this word) who have never had any revealed scripture to fall back upon

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says qayyimah carries an aggregate connotation in this context.
rows.anchor: This aggregate connotation is inherent in the adjective qayyimah as used here (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the common reading that the deniers only separated from error when Muhammad and the Qur’an arrived: not all accepted them, and verse 4 says scriptural communities broke unity after the evidence came.
rows.anchor: This assumption is, however, deficient on two counts: firstly, it is well-known that not all of the erring ones

rows.speaker: Ibn Taymiyyah
rows.claim: Following Ibn Taymiyyah, Asad reads munfakkin as “not abandoned” or condemned by God until people have been shown the right, including through earlier prophets and revelations.
rows.anchor: Ibn Taymiyyah (see Tafsir Sitt Suwar, pp. 391 ff.); and it is his interpretation that I have followed

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir’s definition of those given revelation includes followers of every religious teaching revealed before Muhammad; some commentators restrict it to Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: This definition is general, comprising the followers of all religious teachings revealed before the advent of the Prophet Muhammad (lbn Kathir)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most recipients of earlier revelation strayed from their prophets’ teachings.
rows.anchor: most of them strayed from the teachings of the prophets sent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the sense of hunafa’, Asad refers readers to his note on 2:110.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of hunafa' (sing. hanif), see surah 2, note 110.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakah here has a wider sense than the obligatory tax, so Asad renders it as spending in charity.
rows.anchor: the term zakah has here obviously a wider meaning than the obligatory tax incumbent on practicing] charity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains din here as moral law and refers to his discussion of that connotation on 109:6.
rows.anchor: As regards the connotation of "moral law" in the term din, see note 3 on 109:6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bracketed phrase makes clear that the condemnation concerns denial despite the preceding evidence.
rows.anchor: those who [despite all evidence] are bent on denying the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers reject the self-evident principles of verse 5, which Asad calls the beginning and end of moral law.
rows.anchor: the self-evident principles formulated in the preceding verse as the beginning and the end of all moral law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad applies the warning to those who receive a God-sent prophet, understand the way shown, and consciously refuse it; the Qur’an repeatedly says God does not hold people to wrong belief or action before right and wrong are made clear.
rows.anchor: have consciously refused to follow it: and this is in accord with repeated statements in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound ordinances and moral law are shared by all God-inspired messages, with the Qur’an as their final and most perfect expression.
rows.anchor: common to all God-inspired messages, of which the Qur'an is the final, most perfect expression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad condenses true religion into recognition of God’s oneness and human responsibility, rejecting false values, dubious beliefs, self-overestimation, and superstition, and showing kindness and charity to creatures.
rows.anchor: a cognition of God's oneness and uniqueness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faithful who do good are promised gardens, enduring bliss, and mutual contentment with God.
rows.anchor: well-pleased is God with them

rows.speaker: Itqan
rows.claim: Itqan places the surah most probably in the early Medinan period, while some authorities consider it Meccan.
rows.anchor: MOST PROBABLY revealed in the early part of the Medina period (itqan), although some authorities regard it as a Meccan revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s burdens are what had been hidden in it, including the bodies or remnants of the dead.
rows.anchor: all that was hitherto hidden in it, including the bodies - or the remnants - of the dead

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet explains that on Judgment Day the earth will bear witness to everything people have done; Abu Hurayrah transmits this report, cited by Ibn Hanbal and Tirmidhi.
rows.anchor: the earth will bear witness, as it were, to all that has ever been done by man: an explanation given by the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People appear separately to see their deeds, underscoring each person’s individual and untransferable responsibility; every good or evil deed, however small, is shown.
rows.anchor: to be shown their [past] deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashtatan literally means “as separate entities”; Asad compares the individual appearance with 6:94.
rows.anchor: Lit., "as separate entities" (ashtatan). Cf. 6:94

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: The conventional reading treats the chargers as believers fighting jihad and therefore as laudable imagery.
rows.anchor: believers' fight in God's cause (jihad) and, therefore, represent something highly commendable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s descriptions of sinners’ afterlife suffering are metaphors.
rows.anchor: all Qur'anic descriptions of the sinner's suffering in the hereafter are metaphors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad sends readers to his note 31 on surah 6 for this passage’s explanation.
rows.anchor: See surah 6, note 31.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning may refer to the “hell on earth” people already inhabit, brought about by their own heedless pursuit.
rows.anchor: in which you find yourselves now" - i.e., the "hell on earth" brought about by a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the hereafter people directly see the true nature of past actions and the unavoidable suffering caused by wasting life.
rows.anchor: in the hereafter, through a direct, unequivocal insight into the real nature of one's past doings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term describes anyone who maliciously exposes others’ real or imagined faults.
rows.anchor: everyone who maliciously tries to uncover real or imaginary faults in others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hutamah is one metaphor for the otherworldly suffering included in the concept of hell.
rows.anchor: one of several metaphors for the otherworldly suffering comprised within the concept of "hell'"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire comes from within the sinners’ hearts, pointing to its spiritual nature as they belatedly realize their guilt.
rows.anchor: originating in their hearts - thus clearly alluding to the spiritual nature of the "fire" in the sinners' belated realization

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extended columns overwhelm the sinners with despair.
rows.anchor: in extended columns", i.e., overwhelming with despair

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the campaign against Mecca to 570 CE: Abyssinian Yemen’s viceroy Abrahah built a cathedral at Sana to redirect pilgrimage, then marched to destroy the Kaaba when that failed.
rows.anchor: the Abyssinian campaign against Mecca in the year 570 of the Christian era. Abrahah, the Christian viceroy of the Yemen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahah’s large force included war elephants, astonishing to Arabs; it was destroyed on the march, probably by smallpox or typhus, and Abrahah died on returning to Sana.
rows.anchor: Abrahah's army was totally destroyed on its march

rows.speaker: Ibn Hisham; Ibn Sa'd
rows.claim: Asad cites Ibn Hisham and Ibn Sa’d for the campaign account.
rows.anchor: see Ibn Hisham; also Ibn Sa'd I/1, 55 f.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari; Razi
rows.claim: They take the “pre-ordained” stone blows as punishment set in God’s decree, paralleling the expression in 11:82.
rows.anchor: God's decree (Zamakhshari and Razi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashab literally means the companions of the elephant, with the introduction supplying the historical identification.
rows.anchor: the companions (ashab) of the elephant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjil signifies writing and, figuratively, something decreed by God; Asad therefore takes stones of sijjil as a metaphor for pre-ordained hard blows of punishment.
rows.anchor: hijarah min sijjil is a metaphor for "stone-hard blows of chastisement pre-

rows.speaker: some authorities
rows.claim: Some authorities regard this passage as continued in the next surah, making the two surahs one part.
rows.anchor: This passage is evidently continued in the next surah, which, according to some authorities, is part

rows.speaker: some Companions and scholars of the next generation
rows.claim: Some Companions and later scholars treated al-Fil and Quraysh as one surah; Ubayy ibn Ka‘b’s codex joined them without the basmalah, which Ibn Hajar considered fairly conclusive evidence.
rows.anchor: this surah and the preceding one form , in fact, one entity.

rows.speaker: Umar ibn al-Khattab
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Razi report that Umar recited al-Fil and Quraysh together as a single surah in congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: the two surahs as one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether one surah or two, Quraysh continues al-Fil: God destroyed the elephant army so Quraysh could remain secure.
rows.anchor: whether Al-Fil and Quraysh are one surah or two separate ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The safety of Quraysh is a metonym for the Kaaba’s security and for the faith in God’s oneness associated with it.
rows.anchor: a metonym for the security of the Kabah, the focal point of the Faith based on the concept of God's

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s security refers to safeguarding the Kaaba’s custodians, the tribe in which the Last Prophet would arise; Abrahah’s army was destroyed for this security of monotheism.
rows.anchor: as the custodians of the Kabah and the tribe in the midst of which the Last Prophet, Muhammad, was to appear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The winter and summer journeys were the annual trade caravans to Yemen and Syria, on which Mecca’s prosperity depended.
rows.anchor: the two annual trade caravans - to the Yemen in winter and to Syria in summer - on which the prosperity of Mecca depended

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “House” is the Kaaba; Asad refers to his note on 2:125.
rows.anchor: the Kabah (see note 102 on 2:125)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compares the provision and safety given Quraysh with Abraham’s prayer that the land be secure and its people provided with fruit.
rows.anchor: Make this a land secure, and grant its people fruitful sustenance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads din as objective validity of religion and moral law.
rows.anchor: objective validity in religion as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that the person does not urge others to give food, though Asad adds that he does not do so himself.
rows.anchor: "does not urge", i.e., himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad specifies that the people are knowingly heedless of their prayers.
rows.anchor: who are [knowingly] unmindful of their prayers

rows.speaker: most authorities
rows.claim: Most authorities assign the surah to early Mecca, while Ibn Kathir considers Medina more probable based on Anas ibn Malik’s report of revelation in a mosque.
rows.anchor: Apostle of God was among us in the mosque

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawthar denotes the Prophet’s abundant spiritual good—revelation, knowledge, wisdom, good works, and dignity—and for believers generally the capacity for learning, good works, kindness, inner peace, and dignity.
rows.anchor: al-kawthar obviously relates to the abundant bestowal on the Prophet of all that is good in an abstract, spiritual sense

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Kawthar is an intensive form of kathrah, a term denoting abundance.
rows.anchor: The term kawthar is an intensive form of the noun kathrah (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bracketed “from all that is good” follows the Qamus explanation of abtar as cut off.
rows.anchor: The addition, between brackets, of the phrase "from all that is good" is based on an explanation forthcoming from the Qamus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was revealed shortly after surah 107.
rows.anchor: REVEALED shortly after surah 107.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad’s ma (“that which”) covers both positive ethical commitments, including belief in God and surrender to Him, and false worship and values such as supposed self-sufficiency and compulsive greed.
rows.anchor: all positive concepts and ethical values - e.g., belief in God and the believer's self-surrender to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders din as moral law: obedience to a binding system of established usages or faith, with parallels at 42:21, 95:7, 98:5, and 107:1.
rows.anchor: obedience to a law or to what is conceived as a system of established - and therefore binding - usages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rejection stands so long as the addressees refuse to abandon false values that lead them to deny truth.
rows.anchor: so long as you are unwilling to abandon the false values which cause you to deny the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Din’s primary meaning is obedience; Asad explains the verse as “unto me, my moral law.”
rows.anchor: The primary significance of din is "obedience"; in particular

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed at Mina during the Farewell Pilgrimage in Dhu al-Hijjah 10 AH, An-Nasr was the last complete surah; the only later revelation was 2:281.
rows.anchor: this is unquestionably the last complete surah conveyed by him to the world

rows.speaker: the Prophet's Companions
rows.claim: Because the surah followed the declaration completing the religious law, some Companions inferred Muhammad’s mission was finished and his death near; Bukhari reports this.
rows.anchor: some of the Prophet's Companions concluded that his mission was fulfilled, and that he was about to die (Bukhari)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet said people entered God’s religion in hosts and would later leave it in hosts; Ibn Hanbal transmits this from Jabir, with a similar Abu Hurayrah report in the Mustadrak.
rows.anchor: people have entered God's religion in hosts - and in time they will leave it in hosts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even when many embrace true religion, believers should grow humbler and more aware of their failings rather than self-complacent.
rows.anchor: not to grow self-complacent but should, rather, become more humble and more conscious of his own failings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s religion is surrender to Him, as expressed in 3:19.
rows.anchor: the religion of self-surrender to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the command to praise and seek forgiveness as a warning against pride after victory and large-scale conversion.
rows.anchor: even if people should embrace the true religion in great numbers, a believer ought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This very early Meccan surah, sixth in revelation order, takes its name from its final word and addresses Abu Lahab’s hostility, rooted in arrogance, wealth, and resistance to human equality and judgment by merit; Ibn Zayd is cited by Tabari.
rows.anchor: arrogance, pride in his great wealth

rows.speaker: Baghawi; Muqatil; Zamakhshari; Razi
rows.claim: Abu Lahab’s nickname meant “He of the Flame” and referred to his handsome, glowing face; because it predated Islam, Asad says it was not pejorative.
rows.anchor: expressed in his glowing countenance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab’s real name was Abd al-Uzza.
rows.anchor: The real name of this uncle of the Prophet was Abd al-Uzza.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “fire of lahab” subtly plays on Abu Lahab’s nickname.
rows.anchor: The expression nar dhat lahab is a subtle play upon the meaning of the nickname Abu Lahab

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari; Ikrimah; Mujahid; Qatadah
rows.claim: “Carrier of firewood” is an idiom for secretly carrying evil tales and slander from person to person to kindle hatred.
rows.anchor: a well-known idiomatic expression denoting one who surreptitiously (Zamakhshari; see also Ikrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masad means anything composed of twisted strands, whatever the material.
rows.anchor: The term masad signifies anything that consists of twisted strands, irrespective of the material

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Authentic traditions describe this surah as equivalent to one-third of the Qur’an; Asad considers it likely to be early Meccan.
rows.anchor: the Prophet was wont to describe this surah as "equivalent to one-third of the whole Qur'an"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As-samad is rendered approximately as the Eternal, Uncaused Cause of all being: God is the primary cause and independent eternal being, while all else derives from and depends on Him for origin and continued existence.
rows.anchor: Uncaused Cause of All Being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rendering of as-samad can only approximate its meaning; the term occurs only once in the Qur’an and applies to God alone.
rows.anchor: This rendering gives no more than an approximate meaning of the term as-samad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects God’s uniqueness with notes on 89:3 and 19:77, and says that no human conception or imagination can grasp or compare Him.
rows.anchor: The fact that God is one and unique in every range of human comprehension or imagination

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators date this and the next surah to early Mecca; Razi and Ibn Kathir place them in Medina, while Baghawi, Zamakhshari, and Baydawi leave the question open.
rows.anchor: most of the commentators assign this and the next surah to the early part of the Mecca period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given the scant evidence, Asad judges both surahs probably early Meccan.
rows.anchor: both these surahs are of early Meccan origin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naffathat refers to occult practices such as tying knots while blowing and chanting; its feminine form can refer to human beings (grammatically feminine nafs), not only women, as Zamakhshari and Razi note.
rows.anchor: The feminine gender of naffathat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq means dawn and can metaphorically mean truth emerging after uncertainty; God is thus the source of truth, and taking refuge in Him means striving for truth.
rows.anchor: the emergence of the truth after [a period of] uncertainty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The darkness may mean despair or approaching death; in verses 2–5 evil has both objective and subjective senses, including fear of evil.
rows.anchor: the darkness of despair, or of approaching death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “those who blow upon knots” was a pre-Islamic Arabic idiom for occult endeavors, likely based on knot-tying incantations.
rows.anchor: an idiomatic phrase current in pre-Islamic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse covers the moral and social effects of another person’s envy on one’s life as well as one’s own succumbing to envy.
rows.anchor: the effects - moral and social- which another person's envy may have on one's life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to the preceding surah’s introduction because this surah is closely connected with it.
rows.anchor: with which this one is closely connected

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad interprets jinn as mysterious intangible forces that affect the psyche and blur moral discernment, and also as inner temptations arising from blind hearts, appetites, inherited errors, and false values.
rows.anchor: the "invisible forces" from which we are told to seek refuge with God are the temptations to evil emanating from the blindness of our own hearts

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi takes Satan here in the broadest sense of the term.
rows.anchor: "Satan" in the widest meaning of this designation, as pointed out by Razi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad suggests this is the Qur’an’s earliest mention of the term and concept al-jinnah.
rows.anchor: perhaps the oldest Qur'anic mention of the term and concept of al-jinnah
